newsitem.title: UK: British-U.S. open skies air talks grounded.
newsitem.headline: British-U.S. open skies air talks grounded.

text.p: Talks between Britain and the United States on an agreement to liberalise the trans-Atlantic airline market were postponed for two weeks due to the illness of a senior British negotiator, officials said Monday.
The talks had been due to start in Washington on Tuesday, with representatives from both governments and the major trans-Atlantic carriers.

News of the delay came as the European Commission kicked off a separate series of private hearings in Brussels into the proposed alliance between British Airways and American Airlines, which is conditional on a so-called open skies agreement being reached.
"Our lead official is in (the) hospital so the meeting has been cancelled. The talks have been postponed for a fortnight," a spokesman for the British government said.
British and U.S. carriers expressed regret that the talks had been delayed but officials noted the current round of talks had not been expected to deliver a final open skies agreement.

"It's not damaging. The two sides had been talking informally anyway and this round was never billed as the breakthrough round," one U.S. airline spokesman said. "It was meant to deal with more boring issues like ground handling."

The two sides are believed to have been inching closer, but Scott Yohe, senior vice-president of government affairs at Delta Air Lines Inc., said he believed full agreement was not possible in the current round. He said a deal is likely to emerge in subsequent talks.

Still, a number of other major hurdles need to be cleared. First, the British government wants to try to link the open skies talks with the British Air-American Air alliance. The U.S. wants to keep the talks and consideration of the alliance approval separate.
Britain is still waiting for its competition watchdog, the Office of Fair Trading, to give a final verdict on the alliance after receiving responses from the airline industry.
In particular, airlines are waiting for a clarification on how BA should divest itself of 168 landing slots at London's Heathrow airport -- a condition for the deal to win the regulators' approval.

Whether BA can sell them or must give them away remains a grey area. Britain says the decision lies with the government, but the European Commission says it has final jurisdiction and claims that selling slots is banned under EU law.
Another issue is the British government's argument calling for protection for smaller airlines taking the full brunt of competition under an open skies regime.
Another complicating factor is the chance of a British election being announced in the coming weeks, which could put the talks on the back burner.
